method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO) 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia' (approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022)), 21 claims; LICENCE: No licence statement in the PDF; ranzco.edu site footer reads 'Copyright © RANZCO' with no permission to reproduce (read at the PDF itself (no statement) and https://ranzco.edu/ (site footer)). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines) 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition' (May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025), 11 claims; LICENCE: Copyright © 2025 European Glaucoma Society; no reproduction, copying, translation or storage without written permission; BMJ page stamp: 'Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.' Free to read (Open Access label on the BMJ page). (read at the PDF front matter and page stamps (bjo.bmj.com full-text PDF)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the European Glaucoma Society guideline, 6th edition (2025), paraphrased and hash-anchored, for when to treat ocular hypertension, first treatment (drops or laser trabeculoplasty), drug choice, switching, fixed combinations, target IOP and follow-up. S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. S2's text was extracted with pdftotext and the repeated page stamp lines ('Protected by copyright...', 'Br J Ophthalmol: first published...', 'by guest.') were removed before anchoring. S2 terms, verbatim: 'No parts of this text, illustrations, tables or flowcharts can be reproduced, copied, translated or stored by any means including magnetic, electronic or multimedia formats without written permission of the European Glaucoma Society.' and 'Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.' Used in paraphrase mode under the owner decision that AI-use clauses do not exclude a source.

claims.claim: **Glaucoma is the world's leading cause of preventable, irreversible blindness,** and treating it late risks permanent loss.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Speed of progression varies enormously:** some people never lose useful sight untreated, while in others advanced disease can blind the eye only 3 months after a routine visit found it stable.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most people whose IOP is above the 95th percentile will not develop glaucoma within 5 years,** though the share who do keeps climbing with time.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Starting treatment is a real decision,** given its harms and costs and the fact that some patients would never lose significant vision in their lifetime.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Measure IOP with a calibrated, regularly checked Goldmann applanation tonometer.** Non-contact tonometry is too error-prone for diagnosis or monitoring (mean errors of 0.5–2.9 mmHg against Goldmann in one study) and its readings cannot be swapped for Goldmann values.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Measure corneal thickness too:** Goldmann reads low in thin corneas and high in thick ones, and a thin cornea independently raises the chance that ocular hypertension turns into glaucoma.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not be falsely reassured by a thick cornea:** in a sizeable minority the true pressure inside the eye is as high as the Goldmann figure or higher.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Van Herick grading is not enough to judge the angle; every eye needs assessment for angle closure,** and anyone thought to have it goes to an ophthalmologist because the definitive treatment is surgical. Narrow angles warrant referral as soon as possible, as laser may be needed early.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lower risk** (otherwise healthy eye, normal field and nerve): IOP over 21 but under 28 mmHg with a very thick cornea, a family history of glaucoma, or past blunt eye injury with no after-effects. The optometrist can keep reviewing as needed, and may refer for an opinion.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Higher risk:** IOP over 21 but under 25 mmHg with average corneal thickness; an isolated disc haemorrhage; pseudoexfoliation or pigment dispersion with normal IOP; a rise in measured IOP of 50% or more over time; or drugs that can lift IOP (steroids, antidepressants with narrow angles, topiramate). Keep reviewing, with a much lower bar for referral.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Very high risk — almost always refer, and always if newly identified:** several risk factors; raised IOP from a secondary cause (those drugs, trauma, pseudoexfoliation, pigment dispersion, uveitis, iris or angle new vessels); IOP over 27 mmHg; over 24 with average corneal thickness; over 21 with a thin cornea; or using pressure-lowering drops without any ophthalmologist involved.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Repeated disc haemorrhages count as several risk factors,** moving the patient to very high risk.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **EGS definition of ocular hypertension:** untreated IOP above 21 mmHg with a normal field, disc and nerve fibre layer, an open angle on gonioscopy, and no other eye disease or steroid use. Older age, higher pressure and a thinner cornea predict conversion to glaucoma, and a free OHTS calculator estimates the 5-year risk.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat when the risk of conversion is high,** weighing life expectancy, general health and the chance of meaningful visual loss. Confirm the raised pressure before starting, unless it is very high. As a rule, offer treatment for pressures repeatedly in the high twenties even with no other risk factor; the principles then match those for open-angle glaucoma.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Start with either drops or laser trabeculoplasty, review every 6–12 months at first,** and lengthen the interval if everything stays stable. Assess each person individually and involve them in the decision.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Treatment roughly halves conversion:** in OHTS (1636 patients; goal below 24 mmHg and at least 20% under baseline), 4.4% of treated versus 9.5% of untreated patients developed glaucoma by 5 years, and more than 90% of the untreated had not converted. Waiting to treat raised conversion only when the baseline conversion risk exceeded 13%.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Begin with a single drug,** unless pressure is very high or disease severe; **laser trabeculoplasty is also a good first choice** for mild to moderate open-angle glaucoma or OHT, and one high-quality trial found SLT at least as effective as drops. Pressures in the high 20s or more, or severe disease, may need combined drugs, laser or surgery from the outset.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **LiGHT (718 newly diagnosed, untreated OHT or open-angle glaucoma patients):** 74.2% of the SLT group were at target without drops at 3 years and 69.8% at 6 years; by 6 years fewer SLT eyes needed trabeculectomy (2.4% vs 5.8%) or progressed (19.6% vs 26.8%).
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Prostaglandin analogues lower pressure most and are the usual first medical choice** (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Next come non-selective beta-blockers, then rho-kinase inhibitors, alpha-agonists, selective beta-blockers and topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Preservative-free drops lower pressure no less and are probably easier on the ocular surface, but cost more.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **If the first drug does not work or is not tolerated, switch to another single drug** (same or another class) instead of adding a second.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Add a drug of another class only when a tolerated, effective single drug has not reached target;** a fixed combination is then better than two separate drops (adherence, less preservative). Most contain a beta-blocker, so take care with its systemic contraindications; prostaglandin plus beta-blocker is the commonest pairing. **Do not start with a combination** unless one agent is unlikely to reach target, as in advanced glaucoma or very high pressure.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Set a target IOP when the diagnosis is made and revisit it at each monitoring visit** as the glaucoma, or other eye or general disease, changes.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Anyone an optometrist labels glaucoma or glaucoma suspect should see an ophthalmologist** to confirm the diagnosis and set a plan, with urgency matched to risk and stage. Both the diagnosis and any progression need an ophthalmologist to confirm them.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Follow-up is lifelong** for glaucoma, suspects and ocular hypertension; up to 25% keep losing field despite treatment and close watching.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stable early glaucoma** means repeatable field loss under 6 dB, sparing the central 10 degrees, and unchanged for 3 years. **Advanced glaucoma** (loss over 12 dB or inside 10 degrees of fixation) is generally unsuitable for shared care because functional vision is at stake.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Unstable glaucoma goes back to the treating ophthalmologist promptly:** newly diagnosed with unknown rate of progression, IOP above target or swinging by more than 3 mmHg, structural or field progression within 3 years, disc haemorrhage, drop intolerance, or new eye disease. Laser or surgery may be needed.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acutely raised IOP is an emergency:** blurred vision, nausea and pain, pressure often above 35 mmHg, with a red eye, shallow chamber, fixed pupil, cells or blood in the chamber, or corneal oedema. Causes include acute angle closure, uveitis, rubeosis, pseudoexfoliation and pigment dispersion. Contact an ophthalmologist at once for definitive treatment.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep high-risk patients with the ophthalmologist, not in shared care:** complex or secondary glaucoma (other than pseudoexfoliation or pigment dispersion), glaucoma after eye trauma, one seeing eye, several eye operations, advanced or unstable disease, or IOP above 35 mmHg.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The ophthalmologist writes the plan and sets target pressures,** and is consulted regularly. The arrangement is put in writing, with monitoring intervals and referral timeframes, and the patient gives informed consent.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitoring once glaucoma is excluded (lower-risk suspect):** field test and nerve imaging every 6–12 months under age 80, yearly over 80, and an ophthalmologist review at least every 3–4 years.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Higher-risk suspect:** field and imaging at least 6-monthly under 80 (yearly over 80) and an ophthalmologist at least every 2 years. **Very high-risk suspect:** the same testing, with an ophthalmologist at least every year. Any change prompts immediate re-referral.
claims.locator: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO), 'Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Collaborative Care of glaucoma patients and suspects by ophthalmologists and optometrists in Australia', approved 17 August 2019 (next review 17 August 2022), https://ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Guidelines-for-the-Collaborative-Care-of-Glaucoma-Patients.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **EGS on follow-up (S2):** reviewing ocular hypertension more often than yearly is unlikely to be cost-effective; see people more often for severe or fast-progressing glaucoma, pressure above target or other high-risk factors. Confirming probable progression generally needs at least five field tests (two baseline, three follow-up) over at least two years.
claims.locator: European Glaucoma Society, British Journal of Ophthalmology 109(Suppl 1) (doi 10.1136/bjophthalmol-2025-egsguidelines), 'Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 6th Edition', May 2025; first published online 8 September 2025, https://bjo.bmj.com/content/109/Suppl_1/1, retrieved 2026-09-24
